title: Rahula's verses
hookLine: the son who says he is doubly fortunate, son of the Buddha and heir to the teaching (Theragatha, Rahula)

cards: Give me my inheritance. A small boy says it, walking behind a monk. In the Vinaya's telling, the Buddha has come back to his father's city, and Rahula's mother sends their son after him to ask for what a father owes.
The boy follows, telling the monk he likes the shade he casts. The Buddha doesn't hand him land or gold. He asks Sariputta to ordain the boy.
Much later, Rahula sings about that inheritance himself, in the Theragatha.

teach.b: First, the name. They call me Rahula the fortunate, he says, and I'm fortunate both ways: once because I'm the Buddha's son, once because I've come to see the teaching clearly.
One inheritance by birth, one by practice, and he names both plainly. Second, what the second one asked of him.

teach.h: A FISH IN THE MOUTH OF A TRAP.
teach.b: He describes himself as he was: blinded by pleasures, caught in a net, wrapped in craving, bound by carelessness, like a fish in the mouth of a trap.
Being the Buddha's son, in his own telling, didn't spare him any of that. The first inheritance came free. The second he had to take up.
Third, what he found. The pleasures are thrown off, he says, Mara's bond is cut, craving is pulled out root and all.
He has grown cool, quenched. Fourth, back to the boy in the road.

In the Vinaya, the Buddha reflects that the inheritance the boy asked for brings trouble with it, and chooses to give him another kind, the kind nobody receives by blood. And the text doesn't end on the gift.
Rahula's grandfather, King Suddhodana, comes to the Buddha in pain. He has watched a son leave, and now a grandson.

teach.h: A GRANDFATHER'S GRIEF, A NEW RULE.
teach.b: He asks that no child be ordained without the parents' consent, and the Buddha agrees and makes it a rule. So the second inheritance cost someone something, and the Vinaya keeps that grief on the page.
Doubly fortunate, and the story behind the song shows both sides of the gift.

how: The Vinaya traces its rule of parents' consent before a child is ordained to Rahula's story and his grandfather's grief, and communities that keep the Vinaya keep that rule with it.

o: the Buddha's son's song of two fortunes
the vows Rahula took as a boy novice
the rules the Buddha wrote for children

games.q: Rahula's verses and story: tap the pairs.
p: what he says people call him

s: Rahula says being born the Buddha's son was his whole fortune
he names two fortunes: being the Buddha's son, and coming to see the teaching clearly.
in the Vinaya, the boy asks the Buddha for his inheritance
his mother sends him, and he follows the monk, saying he likes his shade.
the Vinaya leaves the grandfather's grief out of the story
Suddhodana comes to the Buddha in pain and asks that no child be ordained without the parents' consent.

games.q: you're the Buddha. your small son follows you down the road asking for his inheritance. what do you give him?
o: a share of the royal treasure.
nothing: you send him back to his mother.
a different inheritance: you have him ordained.
games.why: in the Vinaya the Buddha decides the boy should have an inheritance that brings no trouble, and asks Sariputta to ordain him. then the grandfather's grief arrives, and a new rule with it.

practice: Bring to mind one thing that came to you by birth, a face, a language, a habit of the hands, a family story, and name it without judging it.
Then name one thing you inherited by choosing it: a practice, a line from a teacher, a way of working you picked up and kept.
If you pray, give thanks for both in your own way; if not, simply hold them side by side, the given and the taken up.

wordCard.voice: Rahula's verses. The Buddha's son, in the Theragatha, calls himself fortunate twice: by birth, and by the teaching he took up. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali dayajja: an inheritance, the thing the boy asks his father for.

carryVoice: Your line: doubly fortunate. One gift came by birth, and one he had to take up. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Vinaya, Mahavagga 1.54 (Rahula's inheritance and Suddhodana's request)
